analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share repair information and tools with independent shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from April 2009 until the Congress ended in January 2011, despite 73 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required car manufacturers to sell or share with vehicle owners and independent repair shops all the diagnostic information, service bulletins, tools, and replacement equipment they give their own dealers. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the requirement, and state attorneys general, consumers, and repair shops could sue violators. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, who could get their vehicles fixed at any shop rather than being pushed to the dealer; independent repair shops, which would get the same data and tools dealers have; and the aftermarket parts and tool industry, which the bill's own text says employs over 5 million people in 495,000 businesses and generates $200 billion in annual sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must provide owners and service providers all information needed to diagnose, service, maintain, or repair a vehicle, including service bulletins and anything sent to dealers directly, indirectly, or wirelessly.
Manufacturers must sell repair tools to owners and all shops on reasonable, non-discriminatory terms, and must let independent tool makers build tools with the same capabilities as dealer-only tools.
The FTC can enforce the requirement as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general, consumers, and repair shops can sue to stop violations and recover damages and attorney fees.
The bill preserves trade secrets, so manufacturers would not have to publish proprietary manufacturing processes unless they already share the information with their dealers.

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers and their franchised dealers, who would lose the advantage of being the only shops with full diagnostic data and dealer-only tools, and some repair revenue that currently flows to dealerships.

drawbacks.text: Carmakers argued that giving outsiders full access to vehicle computers and diagnostic software raises safety, emissions-tampering, and cybersecurity concerns; the bill addressed emissions by barring the FTC from overriding EPA emissions-diagnostic rules but did not address cybersecurity.

Manufacturers invest heavily in developing diagnostic technology, and the bill would require them to hand tools and information to competitors at non-discriminatory terms, which they said could reduce their incentive to build those systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is concrete and ongoing: as cars became rolling computers, the ability to fix them outside the dealership depends on access to data and tools. The main costs fall on automakers and dealers who profit from information control, not on consumers; the safety and emissions concerns are largely handled by the bill's EPA carve-out, though its cybersecurity treatment is thin. On balance the bill trades a concentrated business advantage for broader consumer choice and price competition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the bill on April 22, 2009, with Reps. George Miller and Anna Eshoo as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where the record ends; no further action appears in the bill's history.
Seventy-three House members from both parties cosponsored the bill, including 65 of 253 House Democrats and 8 of 178 House Republicans.

The bill was the 2009 version of the 'right to repair' effort; a nearly identical proposal had also stalled in the 110th Congress, and the underlying dispute was later settled by a 2014 Massachusetts ballot measure and a nationwide industry agreement rather than by federal legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their franchised dealers kept exclusive control of repair data and tools, since no federal law required sharing them during this Congress. Independent shops and car owners remained dependent on voluntary manufacturer programs.

against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee

against.name: Automakers

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 65 of 253 House Democrats and 8 of 178 House Republicans — and the bill died quietly in a committee run by a same-party chair rather than on any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would end carmakers' control over diagnostic data, service tools, and wireless repair information, which supports their dealers' service business. Consumers would gain choice and price competition; manufacturers would lose a revenue edge and some control over proprietary systems.

Dealers' privileged access to information and dealer-only tools is a competitive advantage; the bill would require it to be shared with any shop. Their service departments would face real competition.
Independent shops would get the same data, bulletins, and tools dealers have, letting them fix modern computerized cars. Their gain is car owners' gain in price and choice.

The bill requires manufacturers to share information that lets tool companies build equivalent equipment, supporting an industry the bill text says employs over 5 million people across 495,000 businesses.
